extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, legislators, policymakers, and commentators on liberty and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies John Stuart Mill's principles limiting legitimate social and legal interference with individual conduct (the harm principle and related qualifications) to public-policy questions such as regulation, police powers, trade, and private contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim 1 — individual non-accountability for self-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual is not accountable to society for his actions, in so far as these concern the interests of no person but himself. Advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance by other people if thought necessary by them for their own good, are the only measures by which society can justifiably express its dislike or disapprobation of his conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core rule: purely self-regarding conduct should not be subject to social or legal coercion; social response should be limited to non-coercive measures (advice, persuasion, avoidance). Used as the baseline in weighing specific regulatory proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim 2 — accountability for conduct prejudicial to others
rubrics_metrics.description: For such actions as are prejudicial to the interests of others, the individual is accountable and may be subjected either to social or to legal punishments, if society is of opinion that the one or the other is requisite for its protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conduct harms others, society may legitimately impose sanctions (social or legal). Determination depends on whether such measures are necessary for protection; this principle balances Maxim 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm alone does not automatically justify interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Because damage, or probability of damage, to the interests of others, can alone justify the interference of society, that therefore it always does justify such interference is false. Many legitimate pursuits necessarily cause pain or loss to others; society interferes only when means employed are contrary to general interest—namely, fraud, treachery, or force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between harms that arise from fair competition or legitimate pursuit and harms produced by wrongful methods; only the latter generally justify interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade is a social act but market freedom generally preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade is a social act ... it was once held... to fix prices... but it is now recognised ... that both the cheapness and the good quality of commodities are most effectually provided for by leaving the producers and sellers perfectly free, under the sole check of equal freedom to the buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation of production and trade should be justified by clear countervailing public-interest reasons; restraints are evils qua restraints unless they actually produce the intended public benefits (e.g., prevent fraud, protect health).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish restrictions affecting buyer liberty from those affecting sellers
rubrics_metrics.description: These interferences are objectionable, not as infringements on the liberty of the producer or seller, but on that of the buyer (e.g., prohibition of the importation of opium into China; restriction of sale of poisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy that makes a commodity impossible or difficult to obtain is an intrusion on buyer liberty and requires stronger justification than regulation of sellers' practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate preventive police function with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one of the undisputed functions of government to take precautions against crime before it has been committed ... if a public authority ... sees any one evidently preparing to commit a crime, they are not bound to look on inactive until the crime is committed, but may interfere to prevent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive measures are allowed when there is evident preparation to commit crime, but the preventive function is especially liable to abuse and therefore must be limited and carefully justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of dangerous goods should minimize burden on legitimate uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Precautions ... may be enforced in the sale of articles adapted to be instruments of crime. Labelling the drug with some word expressive of its dangerous character may be enforced without violation of liberty; but to require in all cases the certificate of a medical practitioner, would make it sometimes impossible, always expensive, to obtain the article for legitimate uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer less burdensome safeguards (labelling, 'preappointed evidence' such as registries or witness presence) that deter misuse without denying legitimate access; avoid blanket requirements that hinder lawful uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preappointed evidence / registration as a proportionate safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The seller might be required to enter into a register the exact time of the transaction, the name and address of the buyer, the precise quality and quantity sold; to ask the purpose for which it was wanted, and record the answer he received ... the presence of some third person might be required ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative formalities that create accountability and make illicit use more detectable are legitimate means of preventing misuse while preserving access for legitimate buyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted personal legal restrictions where justified by prior conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: I should deem it perfectly legitimate that a person, who had once been convicted of any act of violence to others under the influence of drink, should be placed under a special legal restriction, personal to himself; that if he were afterwards found drunk, he should be liable to a penalty ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State may impose individualized constraints on persons with demonstrated propensity to cause harm (recidivists), even when the underlying conduct (e.g., drinking) is ordinarily self-regarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity of conduct can change its permissible regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many acts which, being directly injurious only to the agents themselves, ought not to be legally interdicted, but which, if done publicly, are a violation of good manners and coming thus within the category of offences against others may rightfully be prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private self-regarding behaviour remains protected; public manifestations that offend decency or others' interests can be regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to counsel and to instigate self-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: If people must be allowed, in whatever concerns only themselves, to act as seems best to themselves ... they must equally be free to consult with one another about what is fit to be so done; to exchange opinions, and give and receive suggestions. Whatever it is permitted to do, it must be permitted to advise to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech advising self-regarding conduct should generally be tolerated; the question becomes difficult when the adviser derives personal benefit and operates as an interested promoter of harmful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special scrutiny for commercial promoters of harmful practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When the instigator derives a personal benefit from his advice; when he makes it his occupation, for subsistence or pecuniary gain, to promote what society and the state consider to be an evil ... Ought this to be interfered with, or not? ... There are arguments on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercialized inducement (pimps, gambling-house keepers, sellers with pecuniary interest in excess) lies on the boundary between toleration and permissible suppression; regulation of such intermediaries may be defensible even if the principal actors are tolerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate sellers when their interest promotes public harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest of these dealers in promoting intemperance is a real evil, and justifies the State in imposing restrictions and requiring guarantees, which but for that justification would be infringements of legitimate liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sellers' commercial incentives meaningfully contribute to social harm, the State may impose constraints (licensing, guarantees) targeted at sellers rather than banning private consumption outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal policy selection: tax indirect consumption according to what consumers can spare
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation for fiscal purposes is absolutely inevitable ... It is hence the duty of the State to consider, in the imposition of taxes, what commodities the consumers can best spare; and, a fortiori, to select in preference those of which it deems the use, beyond a very moderate quantity, to be positively injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect taxes are permissible; the state should choose items for taxation that both raise revenue and (when useful) disincentivize harmful consumption, up to the revenue-maximizing point if revenue is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and policing of public places of sale for public-order reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fit to confine the power of selling these commodities (at least for consumption on the spot) to persons of known or vouched-for respectability of conduct; to make such regulations respecting hours of opening and closing as may be requisite for public surveillance, and to withdraw the licence if breaches of the peace repeatedly take place through the connivance or incapacity of the keeper of the house ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions aimed at preventing public disorder (licensing, hours, withdrawal on breaches) are legitimate; restrictions intended solely to make access more difficult (limiting number of houses to reduce temptation) are in principle unjustifiable unless other conditions warrant it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on enforceability of voluntary engagements that alienate essential rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An engagement by which a person should sell himself, or allow himself to be sold, as a slave, would be null and void ... The principle of freedom cannot require that he should be free not to be free. It is not freedom, to be allowed to alienate his freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts or promises that result in permanent alienation of fundamental liberties (selling oneself into slavery) are void; freedom does not extend to surrendering the very conditions that justify liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations for contracts affecting personal relations and third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person ... has encouraged another to rely upon his continuing to act in a certain way ... a new series of moral obligations arises ... if the relation between two contracting parties has been followed by consequences to others ... obligations arise on the part of both the contracting parties towards those third persons ... they necessarily make a great difference in the moral freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where parties are free to dissolve personal engagements, moral and sometimes legal obligations to third parties (dependents, children) constrain the justice of unilateral retraction; such obligations must be weighed in deciding enforceability and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective self-regulation among consenting parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of the individual, in things wherein the individual is alone concerned, implies a corresponding liberty in any number of individuals to regulate by mutual agreement such things as regard them jointly, and regard no persons but themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups of consenting adults may freely regulate their joint affairs without state interference, so long as third parties are not harmed and consent is genuine; the state should respect mutually agreed private arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-intervention between communities absent aggression or third-party harm
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as the sufferers by the bad law do not invoke assistance from other communities, I cannot admit that persons entirely unconnected with them ought to step in and require that a condition of things with which all who are directly interested appear to be satisfied, should be put an end to because it is a scandal to persons some thousands of miles distant, who have no part or concern in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External coercive interference (military or forcible 'civilizing' expeditions) against another community's internal practices is illegitimate unless those practices aggress others or third parties ask for assistance; persuasion and non-coercive opposition (missionaries, argument) are the proper channels.
